rationale: A wins because it keeps the four real stories separate: the diner receipt, the worker shift, the rollout math, and the margin question. Its best line, "100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation," is a sharp inference framed as a question reporters will ask, not a fact Chipotle gets to self-award. B is useful, but "Two robots, one bowl: Chipotle is automating the assembly line from both ends" turns one rollout plus one test into a category thesis wearing a fake mustache.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" is plausible, but not sourced in the update; it needs outside evidence or softer framing.
"This beat has watched kitchen robots stall at the demo stage" adds industry context the update did not provide; fine as reporter intuition, weak as a claim.

"100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation" is the right skeptical question, but it still needs cost, volume, and margin data before it becomes more than inference.
gaps_in_B: "it's the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format" is invented. The update says Autocado is rolling out and Digital Makeline is testing; it does not prove a full-line automation architecture.
"Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it" is consultant vapor. No competitor/operator evidence was supplied.
"the two statements were made together and can only be examined together right now" overforces the peg. They can be examined together, but the update does not make the causal link.

"Chipotle's price freeze and what it means for household budgets" is refused too aggressively; with a national chain holding menu prices flat, A's consumer-price lane is valid if it gets basket and scope proof.
